'''Woccon''' was one of two attested [[Catawban languages|Catawban]] (also known as Eastern Siouan) languages of what is now the [[Eastern United States]]. Together with the [[Western Siouan languages]], they formed the [[Siouan languages|Siouan language family]]. It is attested only in a vocabulary of 143 words, printed in a 1709 compilation by English colonist [[John Lawson (explorer)|John Lawson]] of Carolina.<ref>Lawson, John (1709). “A vocabulary of Woccon”, in ''A New Voyage to Carolina; Containing the Exact Description and Natural History of That Country: Together with the Present State Thereof. And a Journal of a Thousand Miles, Travel’d Thro’ Several Nations of Indians. Giving a Particular Account of Their Customs, Manners, &c.'' View online.</ref>{{non-primary source needed|date=June 2025}} The Woccon people that Lawson encountered have been considered by some scholars, including [[John R. Swanton]], to have possibly been a late subdivision of the [[Waccamaw]].<ref name=swanton/> Contemporary [[linguists]] and researchers have been unable to resolve whether Woccon directly represents the language of the historic Waccamaw people, as opposed to representing a related Catawban language.<ref name=Passmore/>

The Woccon are believed to have been decimated as a people during the [[Tuscarora War]] in the Carolinas with English colonists in 1713. Survivors were likely absorbed into the [[Tuscarora people|Tuscarora]], an Iroquoian-speaking people, who subsequently migrated north to New York, settling with the five nations of the [[Iroquois Confederacy]] by 1722 and being accepted as the sixth. Under these pressures, the Woccon language is believed to have become extinct in the eighteenth century. Some descendants of Woccon ancestry possibly survive in the Southeast as well as Canada, where the Six Nations of the Iroquois migrated after the American Revolutionary War.<ref>Carter, R. (1980). "The Woccon Language of North Carolina: Its Genetic Affiliations and Historical Significance", in ''International Journal of American Linguistics'', Volume 46, Number 3. https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/abs/10.1086/465652?journalCode=ijal</ref>

==Documentation==
The Woccon language is poorly attested, with all known material originating from a single colonial source. The primary record is a 143-word list compiled by John Lawson in 1711, which includes vocabulary from [[Tuscarora language|Tuskeruro]], [[Carolina Algonquian language|Pampticough]], and Woccon. Additional attestations come from an 1806 list by Adelung and Vater, which includes 16 German-Woccon glosses. However, researchers have noted that several terms in this list appear to duplicate entries from Lawson and may reflect confusion between Woccon and [[Catawba language|Catawba]] terms.<ref name=Passmore/>

The linguistic data suffers from inconsistencies and inaccuracies. Lawson, for example, claimed that Woccon lacked "l" and "f" sounds, yet included such letters in his transcriptions. The language documentation was recorded by non-native speakers and filtered through colonial perspectives, further complicating efforts to assess accuracy. Scholars working with these records have pointed out that the limited and inconsistent nature of the data makes identifying grammatical patterns or establishing definitive linguistic relationships extremely difficult. As such, Woccon remains a fragmentarily attested and ambiguously classified language within the Eastern Siouan branch.<ref name=Passmore/>

==Revival efforts==

In 2021 the [[Living Tongues Institute for Endangered Languages]] assisted the [[Cape Fear Band of Skarure and Woccon Indians]] to build a 'Living Dictionary' for Woccon as part of an effort to revive the language.<ref name="LTI">{{cite web |title=Collaboration with the Skarure Woccon to develop the first-ever Woccon Living Dictionary |url=https://livingtongues.org/woccon-living-dictionary/ |website=Living Tongues Institute for Endangered Languages |access-date=24 April 2025 |date=16 October 2021}}</ref> However, this group is not [[state-recognized tribe|state-recognized]] by North Carolina or [[List of federally recognized tribes in the United States|federally recognized]] by the [[Bureau of Indian Affairs]] as being descended from the [[Cape Fear Indians|Cape Fear]], [[Tuscarora people|Tuscarora]], or the [[Waccamaw]].<ref>{{cite web |title=NC Tribal Communities |url=https://ncadmin.nc.gov/public/american-indians/nc-tribal-communities |website=ncadmin.nc.gov |access-date=20 October 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=About NC Native Communities |url=https://americanindiancenter.unc.edu/resources/about-nc-native-communities/ |website=American Indian Center |access-date=20 October 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Indian Entities Recognized by and Eligible To Receive Services From the United States Bureau of Indian Affairs |url=https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2022/01/28/2022-01789/indian-entities-recognized-by-and-eligible-to-receive-services-from-the-united-states-bureau-of |website=federalregister.gov |date=28 January 2022 |access-date=20 October 2022}}</ref> The group's assertions of lineage have been noted by [[EBSCO Information Services]] to be unverified by credible historians or anthropologists.<ref name="ebsco">{{cite web |title=Cape Fear |url=https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/agriculture-and-agribusiness/cape-fear |website=EBSCOhost.com |access-date=6 April 2025 |language=en}}</ref> The state-recognized [[Waccamaw Siouan Indians]] of North Carolina and the [[Waccamaw Indian People]] of South Carolina were not included in the Living Dictionary project initiated by the Living Tongues Institute during the process of assembling the revitalization dictionary.<ref name=LTI/> 

Since 2023, the state-recognized Waccamaw Siouan have undertaken grassroots efforts to revive the Woccon language, which they identify as the ancestral language of their community.<ref name="Passmore">{{cite journal |last1=Passmore |first1=Elizabeth |last2=Sayers |first2=Addie |last3=Bradley |first3=Julien |last4=Lomboy |first4=Ashley |title=Reviving Waccamaw Siouan: Reconciling ethics, Indigenous epistemologies, and colonial data archives |journal=Proceedings of the Linguistic Society of America |date=15 May 2024 |volume=9 |issue=1 |pages=5717 |doi=10.3765/plsa.v9i1.5717 |url=https://journals.linguisticsociety.org/proceedings/index.php/PLSA/article/view/5717|doi-access=free }}</ref> In partnership with linguists from the [[University of North Carolina Wilmington]], the tribe has engaged in a reclamation project using John Lawson's colonial-era word list.<ref name=Passmore/> The project incorporates decolonial methodologies that prioritize Indigenous [[Epistemology|epistemologies]], reject traditional models of scholarly ownership, and center tribal authority over linguistic decisions.<ref name=Passmore/> As part of this initiative, the Waccamaw Siouan have advocated renaming the historic language to “Waccamaw Siouan,” in order to reflect their contemporary identity and attempts to assert historical and cultural continuity.<ref name=Passmore/> The Waccamaw Siouan’s past position has included public proclamations declining to recognize others as tribal entities or descendants of the historic Waccamaw people, including the state-recognized Waccamaw Indian People of South Carolina.<ref name="crediford">{{cite book |last1=Crediford |first1=Gene J. |title=Those Who Remain: A Photographer's Memoir of South Carolina Indians |date=2009 |publisher=The University of Alabama Press |location=Tuscaloosa, AL |isbn=9780817355180 |pages=122}}</ref> This stance has contributed to the tribe’s claims of exclusivity over the Woccon language and its revitalization.<ref name=Passmore/>

While some scholars, such as [[John R. Swanton]], have historically suggested that Woccon and Waccamaw may refer to the same people or language, this identification remains a matter of scholarly debate.<ref name=swanton/><ref name=Passmore/> The historical record is limited and contains inconsistencies in attribution, terminology, and linguistic content.<ref name=Passmore/> As noted by linguists and researchers involved in the Waccamaw Siouan revival project, the question of whether Woccon directly represents the language of the historic  Waccamaw people, as opposed to being a related language, remains academically unresolved.<ref name=Passmore/> As such, the current revival efforts proceed under a framework that emphasizes tribal sovereignty and cultural continuity, even as the linguistic classification of the language remains inconclusive.<ref name=Passmore/>
